articles.description:
LioranDB TypeScript Series #5: Cursors, Query Shaping and Full-Text Search



LioranDB TypeScript Series: Build with a developer-first document database powered by Rust and designed for TypeScript.
Calling find() doesn't simply give you an array.
It gives you a FindCursor.
That distinction becomes useful as queries grow.
const cursor = users
  .find({ active: true })
  .sort({ email: 1 })
  .limit(20);

Execute it:
const usersArray = await cursor.toArray();

Or iterate over it:
for await (const user of users.find({ active: true })) {
  console.log(user);
}

FindCursor supports:
filter()
limit()
skip()
sort()
project()

For example:
const results = await users
  .find({ active: true })
  .project({
    email: 1,
    age: 1,
  })
  .sort({
    age: -1,
  })
  .skip(20)
  .limit(20)
  .toArra…

const client = await LioranDBClient.connect(process.env.URI!);

There's quite a bit happening underneath it.
Let's unpack it.
A typical local URI looks like:
liorandb://admin:password@127.0.0.1:27018/default

LioranDB understands multiple schemes:
liorandb://
liorandb+http://
liorandb+https://
http://
https://
grpc://

For example:

or:
liorandb+https://admin:password@db.example.com/default

articles.author: Walker Wolfson
articles.description:
I've been logging every push-up, pull-up, dip, and set of squats into Nickels & Dimes, the calisthenics tracker I built, for a few weeks now. Here's what one actual week of my own data looks like, and a couple things tracking it consistently has changed about how I train.
Last 7 days:
466 total reps
245 push-ups
145 pull-ups
40 sit-ups
36 dips
Lifetime PRs so far:
Push-ups: 185
Squats: 210
Dips: 45
Pull-ups: 22
Chin-ups: 15
Plank: 3:20
Dead-hang: 1:45
Burpees: 60
Muscle-ups: 4
Pistol squats: 8
I built Nickels & Dimes because I was logging reps in my phone's Notes app, and every tracker I tried was either bloated with coaching programs I didn't want, or built for barbell lifting with bodyweight reps bolted on as an afterthought.
The thing that's actually changed my training isn't the app itself, it's that I can see the totals instead of guessing. Some days I train hard, some days I don't train at all, and seeing that pattern laid out instead of just feeling vaguely inconsistent has made me actually fix it.
The other piece that's mattered more than I expected: clubs. You can create a public or private club and rank total reps against friends every month. Competing against people I actually know has done more for my consistency than any streak counter or badge system I've used in other apps.
It's free, live at nickelsanddimes.app, built with Next.js, Supabase, and Prisma. Genuinely curious what other people's numbers look like if you track bodyweight training rigorously -- and what's actually kept you consistent.
articles.title: What a Week of Tracking Calisthenics Reps Actually Looks Like

articles.author: Daniel Isaac E
articles.description:
Introduction
The first finding wasn't critical.
It wasn't even particularly interesting.
There was no SQL Injection.
No Remote Code Execution.
No authentication bypass.
Just an API endpoint that shouldn't have been exposed.
On its own, it looked like a low-severity finding.
But penetration testing isn't about collecting vulnerabilities.
It's about understanding what those vulnerabilities can reach.
A forgotten endpoint can expose functionality.
That functionality can reveal an authorization weakness.
That weakness can provide access to another service.
That service can trust information it shouldn't.
And suddenly, several ordinary findings can become a serious attack path.
The endpoint wasn't the vulnerability.
The attack chain was.
The Problem With Looking at Vulnerabilities Individually
…
